claim: CFTR is the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients.
source: CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, is opened by ATP binding to two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), but pore-domain mutations may also impair gating.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CFTR and cystic fibrosis.

claim: CFTR is opened by ATP binding to two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs).
source: CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, is opened by ATP binding to two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), but pore-domain mutations may also impair gating.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: Pore-domain mutations may impair CFTR gating.
source: CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, is opened by ATP binding to two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), but pore-domain mutations may also impair gating.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR mutations.

claim: ATP-bound NBDs dimerize occluding two nucleotides at interfacial binding sites.
source: ATP-bound NBDs dimerize occluding two nucleotides at interfacial binding sites; one site hydrolyzes ATP, the other is inactive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NBD dimerization in ABC proteins.

claim: One ATP binding site hydrolyzes ATP, the other is inactive.
source: ATP-bound NBDs dimerize occluding two nucleotides at interfacial binding sites; one site hydrolyzes ATP, the other is inactive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the asymmetric ATP sites in CFTR.

claim: The pore opens upon tightening of the catalytic site.
source: The pore opens upon tightening, and closes upon disengagement, of the catalytic site following ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: The pore closes upon disengagement of the catalytic site following ATP hydrolysis.
source: The pore opens upon tightening, and closes upon disengagement, of the catalytic site following ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: Marked asynchrony of motion in the two ATP sites reveals their distinct roles in channel gating.
source: Marked asynchrony of motion in the two ATP sites reveals their distinct roles in channel gating.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on Φ value analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an incurable, devastating inherited disease caused by mutations in the CF Transmembrane Conductance regulator (CFTR) chloride ion channel.
source: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an incurable, devastating inherited disease caused by mutations in the CF Transmembrane Conductance regulator (CFTR) chloride ion channel (Riordan et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Riordan et al., 1989.

claim: A large number of mutations identified in CF patients scatter throughout the entire protein sequence and cause defects in protein synthesis, maturation, stability, channel gating, and/or anion permeation through the open channel pore.
source: A large number of mutations identified in CF patients scatter throughout the entire protein sequence and cause defects in protein synthesis, maturation, stability, channel gating, and/or anion permeation through the open channel pore (O'Sullivan and Freedman, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to O'Sullivan and Freedman, 2009.

claim: Small molecule drugs that target the CFTR protein and rectify either processing ('correctors') or gating defects ('potentiators') have proven beneficial for some CF patients carrying specific mutations in recent clinical trials.
source: In recent clinical trials small molecule drugs that target the CFTR protein and rectify either processing ('correctors') or gating defects ('potentiators') have proven beneficial for some CF patients carrying specific mutations (Ramsey et al., 2011), underscoring the importance of understanding the structure and mechanism of this disease-associated protein at a molecular level.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramsey et al., 2011.

claim: CFTR belongs to the large family of ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) proteins.
source: CFTR belongs to the large family of ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) proteins (Riordan et al., 1989), most of which function as active transporters (Dean and Annilo, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Riordan et al., 1989.

claim: Most ABC proteins function as active transporters.
source: CFTR belongs to the large family of ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) proteins (Riordan et al., 1989), most of which function as active transporters (Dean and Annilo, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Dean and Annilo, 2005.

claim: A conserved molecular mechanism that involves ATP binding and hydrolysis drives opening and closing (gating) of the CFTR pore and substrate translocation through other ABC proteins.
source: A conserved molecular mechanism that involves ATP binding and hydrolysis drives opening and closing (gating) of the CFTR pore and substrate translocation through other ABC proteins (Li et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Li et al., 1996.

claim: The exceptional resolution of single-channel patch-clamp recordings makes CFTR a model ABC protein eminently suitable for molecular-level biophysical studies.
source: The exceptional resolution of single-channel patch-clamp recordings makes CFTR a model ABC protein eminently suitable for molecular-level biophysical studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical capabilities of single-channel patch-clamp recordings.

claim: ABC proteins are built from two homologous halves each containing a transmembrane domain (TMD) and a cytosolic nucleotide binding domain (NBD).
source: ABC proteins are built from two homologous halves each containing a transmembrane domain (TMD) and a cytosolic nucleotide binding domain (NBD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC protein structure.

claim: In CFTR the two canonical halves are linked by the unique regulatory (R) domain which must be either phosphorylated by cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) or deleted to allow channel gating.
source: In CFTR these two canonical halves are linked by the unique regulatory (R) domain which must be either phosphorylated by cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) (Anderson et al., 1991), or deleted (Figure 1A) (Csanády et al., 2000) to allow channel gating.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Anderson et al., 1991 and Csanády et al., 2000.

claim: The highly conserved NBD fold comprises an alpha/beta 'head' subdomain harboring the Walker A and B motifs, and an alpha-helical 'tail' subdomain which contains the ABC-specific 'signature' sequence.
source: The highly conserved NBD fold comprises an alpha/beta 'head' subdomain harboring the Walker A and B motifs, and an alpha-helical 'tail' subdomain which contains the ABC-specific 'signature' sequence (Hung et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hung et al., 1998.

claim: Binding of ATP to the Walker motifs in each of the two NBDs promotes their association into a tight head-to-tail dimer that occludes the two bound ATP molecules at interfacial binding sites formed by the Walker motifs of one NBD and the signature motif of the other.
source: Binding of ATP to the Walker motifs in each of the two NBDs promotes their association into a tight head-to-tail dimer that occludes the two bound ATP molecules at interfacial binding sites formed by the Walker motifs of one NBD and the signature motif of the other (Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Smith et al., 2002.

claim: NBD dimers are extremely stable but dissociate following ATP hydrolysis.
source: Such NBD dimers are extremely stable but dissociate following ATP hydrolysis (Moody et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Moody et al., 2002 and Smith et al., 2002.

claim: Formation/disruption of the NBD dimer, communicated to the TMDs through an interface formed by four short coupling helices (CH1-4), drives the major conformational rearrangements of the substrate translocation pathway.
source: Formation/disruption of the NBD dimer, communicated to the TMDs through an interface formed by four short coupling helices (CH1-4, Figure 1A, violet loops), drives the major conformational rearrangements of the substrate translocation pathway (Locher, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Locher, 2009.

claim: The closed-pore CFTR structure is inward facing.
source: The closed-pore CFTR structure is inward facing (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017), whereas the open-pore structure, with dimerized NBDs, likely resembles the outward-facing TMD conformation of ABC proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang and Chen, 2016 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The open-pore structure, with dimerized NBDs, likely resembles the outward-facing TMD conformation of ABC proteins.
source: The closed-pore CFTR structure is inward facing (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017), whereas the open-pore structure, with dimerized NBDs, likely resembles the outward-facing TMD conformation of ABC proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge of ABC proteins.

claim: In a subset of ABC transporters, including CFTR, only one of the two composite sites is catalytically active, whereas the other contains non-canonical substitutions at several key residues that impair ATPase activity.
source: In a subset of ABC transporters, including CFTR, only one of the two composite sites is catalytically active, whereas the other contains non-canonical substitutions at several key residues that impair ATPase activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about asymmetric ABC proteins.

claim: In CFTR the degenerate ATP site ('non-catalytic site 1', formed by NBD1 Walker motifs and NBD2 signature sequence), keeps ATP bound but unhydrolyzed throughout several gating cycles.
source: In CFTR that degenerate ATP site ('non-catalytic site 1', formed by NBD1 Walker motifs and NBD2 signature sequence), keeps ATP bound but unhydrolyzed throughout several gating cycles (Aleksandrov et al., 2002; Basso et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Aleksandrov et al., 2002 and Basso et al., 2003.

claim: The precise range of gating-related movements in non-catalytic site 1 is unclear.
source: The precise range of gating-related movements in non-catalytic site 1 is unclear (Tsai et al., 2010b; Szollosi et al., 2011; Chaves and Gadsby, 2015), but mutations here impair ATP hydrolysis at the catalytic site 2 (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999), affect channel gating (Tsai et al., 2010a; Csanády et al., 2013), and may cause CF (e.g., G1349D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsai et al., 2010b; Szollosi et al., 2011; and Chaves and Gadsby, 2015.

claim: Mutations in non-catalytic site 1 impair ATP hydrolysis at the catalytic site 2.
source: The precise range of gating-related movements in non-catalytic site 1 is unclear (Tsai et al., 2010b; Szollosi et al., 2011; Chaves and Gadsby, 2015), but mutations here impair ATP hydrolysis at the catalytic site 2 (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999), affect channel gating (Tsai et al., 2010a; Csanády et al., 2013), and may cause CF (e.g., G1349D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramjeesingh et al., 1999.

claim: Mutations in non-catalytic site 1 affect channel gating.
source: The precise range of gating-related movements in non-catalytic site 1 is unclear (Tsai et al., 2010b; Szollosi et al., 2011; Chaves and Gadsby, 2015), but mutations here impair ATP hydrolysis at the catalytic site 2 (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999), affect channel gating (Tsai et al., 2010a; Csanády et al., 2013), and may cause CF (e.g., G1349D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsai et al., 2010a and Csanády et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in non-catalytic site 1 may cause CF (e.g., G1349D).
source: The precise range of gating-related movements in non-catalytic site 1 is unclear (Tsai et al., 2010b; Szollosi et al., 2011; Chaves and Gadsby, 2015), but mutations here impair ATP hydrolysis at the catalytic site 2 (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999), affect channel gating (Tsai et al., 2010a; Csanády et al., 2013), and may cause CF (e.g., G1349D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the example mutation G1349D.

claim: Resolving the relative timing of motions in various protein regions allows the molecular forces that drive protein conformational rearrangements to be understood.
source: Resolving the relative timing of motions in various protein regions allows the molecular forces that drive protein conformational rearrangements to be understood.
evidence: This is a general principle of protein biophysics.

claim: The structural organization of the transition (T) state for channel opening may shed light on the sources of molecular strain that underly the large Gibbs energy of this highest-energy intermediate conformation, which rate limits the overall transition.
source: In particular, the structural organization of the transition (T) state for channel opening may shed light on the sources of molecular strain that underly the large Gibbs energy of this highest-energy intermediate conformation, which rate limits the overall transition (Csanády et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2006.

claim: T-state structures cannot be studied by standard structural approaches, as their life times fall into the sub-microsecond range.
source: Such T-state structures cannot be studied by standard structural approaches, as their life times fall into the sub-microsecond range (Chakrapani and Auerbach, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chakrapani and Auerbach, 2005.

claim: Relative timing of motions of a given channel position is reported by its Φ value, the slope of a log-log plot of the opening rate constant (kCO) as a function of the closed-open equilibrium constant (Keq = kCO/kOC) for a series of point substitutions (Brønsted plot).
source: However, relative timing of motions of a given channel position is reported by its Φ value, the slope of a log-log plot of the opening rate constant (kCO) as a function of the closed-open equilibrium constant (Keq = kCO/kOC) for a series of point substitutions (Brønsted plot).
evidence: This is an established method in protein biophysics.

claim: For the opening step of a simple idealized two-state channel with a single intervening T state, Φ is a measure of how far the conformation of the position has progressed along the reaction coordinate in the T state (0≤Φ ≤1).
source: For the opening step of a simple idealized two-state channel with a single intervening T state, Φ is a measure of how far the conformation of the position has progressed along the reaction coordinate in the T state (0≤Φ ≤1).
evidence: This is an established principle of Φ value analysis.

claim: For a position that moves very late, and is still in its closed-like conformation in the T-state (Φ = 0), perturbations affect closing but not opening rate.
source: At the other extreme, for a position that moves very late, and is still in its closed-like conformation in the T-state (Φ = 0), perturbations affect closing but not opening rate (Auerbach, 2007).
evidence: This is an established principle of Φ value analysis supported by citation to Auerbach, 2007.

claim: The overall closed-to-open conformational change of large ion-channel proteins is best described by a sequence of conformational steps across a chain of high-energy intermediary states (the 'transition-state ensemble').
source: In reality, the overall closed-to-open conformational change of large ion-channel proteins is best described by a sequence of conformational steps across a chain of high-energy intermediary states (the 'transition-state ensemble'), and the Φ value of a position reports whether its perturbations affect early (large Φ) or late (small Φ) steps within that chain of events.
evidence: This is an established principle in protein biophysics.

claim: The Φ value of a position reports whether its perturbations affect early (large Φ) or late (small Φ) steps within the chain of conformational events.
source: In reality, the overall closed-to-open conformational change of large ion-channel proteins is best described by a sequence of conformational steps across a chain of high-energy intermediary states (the 'transition-state ensemble'), and the Φ value of a position reports whether its perturbations affect early (large Φ) or late (small Φ) steps within that chain of events.
evidence: This is an established principle of Φ value analysis.

claim: On the plausible assumption that perturbation of a position affects the microscopic step during which the position undergoes a rearrangement, but not steps during which it remains static, the Φ value is reasonably interpreted to reflect relative timing of movements.
source: However, on the plausible assumption that perturbation of a position affects the microscopic step during which the position undergoes a rearrangement, but not steps during which it remains static, the Φ value is reasonably interpreted to reflect relative timing of movements even in such cases (Zhou et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2005.

claim: Φ value analysis requires equilibrium.
source: Because Φ value analysis requires equilibrium (Csanády, 2009), it can be applied to CFTR pore opening only in the presence of a background mutation (Figure 1A–B, red star) that disrupts ATP hydrolysis at catalytic site 2 (Figure 1B, red cross), thus reducing gating in saturating ATP to a simple closed-open equilibrium (C1↔O1; Figure 1B, red box).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády, 2009.

claim: Φ value analysis can be applied to CFTR pore opening only in the presence of a background mutation that disrupts ATP hydrolysis at catalytic site 2, thus reducing gating in saturating ATP to a simple closed-open equilibrium.
source: Because Φ value analysis requires equilibrium (Csanády, 2009), it can be applied to CFTR pore opening only in the presence of a background mutation (Figure 1A–B, red star) that disrupts ATP hydrolysis at catalytic site 2 (Figure 1B, red cross), thus reducing gating in saturating ATP to a simple closed-open equilibrium (C1↔O1; Figure 1B, red box).
evidence: This is a methodological requirement based on the need for equilibrium conditions.

claim: The background construct cut-ΔR(D1370N) contains a mutation of the NBD2 Walker B aspartate that disrupts ATP hydrolysis and removal of the R domain obviates the need for prior phosphorylation.
source: These conditions are satisfied in a background construct (Sorum et al., 2015) in which mutation of the NBD2 Walker B aspartate disrupts ATP hydrolysis and removal of the R domain obviates the need for prior phosphorylation (cut-ΔR(D1370N); Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: In the cut-ΔR(D1370N) background, Φ value analysis detected a clear temporal gradient in opening-related movements which spreads along the longitudinal, cytoplasmic to extracellular, protein axis from catalytic site 2 towards the pore.
source: In this background, Φ value analysis detected a clear temporal gradient in opening-related movements which spreads along the longitudinal, cytoplasmic to extracellular, protein axis from catalytic site 2 towards the pore (Figure 1C): in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized (Φ ~ 1 for position 1246), the NBD-TMD interface is on the move (Φ ~ 0.5 for position 275), whereas the pore is still shut (Φ ~ 0.2 for position 348), suggesting strain in the region of the main CF locus (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: In the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized (Φ ~ 1 for position 1246).
source: In this background, Φ value analysis detected a clear temporal gradient in opening-related movements which spreads along the longitudinal, cytoplasmic to extracellular, protein axis from catalytic site 2 towards the pore (Figure 1C): in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized (Φ ~ 1 for position 1246), the NBD-TMD interface is on the move (Φ ~ 0.5 for position 275), whereas the pore is still shut (Φ ~ 0.2 for position 348), suggesting strain in the region of the main CF locus (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: The NBD-TMD interface is on the move in the T state (Φ ~ 0.5 for position 275).
source: In this background, Φ value analysis detected a clear temporal gradient in opening-related movements which spreads along the longitudinal, cytoplasmic to extracellular, protein axis from catalytic site 2 towards the pore (Figure 1C): in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized (Φ ~ 1 for position 1246), the NBD-TMD interface is on the move (Φ ~ 0.5 for position 275), whereas the pore is still shut (Φ ~ 0.2 for position 348), suggesting strain in the region of the main CF locus (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: The pore is still shut in the T state (Φ ~ 0.2 for position 348).
source: In this background, Φ value analysis detected a clear temporal gradient in opening-related movements which spreads along the longitudinal, cytoplasmic to extracellular, protein axis from catalytic site 2 towards the pore (Figure 1C): in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized (Φ ~ 1 for position 1246), the NBD-TMD interface is on the move (Φ ~ 0.5 for position 275), whereas the pore is still shut (Φ ~ 0.2 for position 348), suggesting strain in the region of the main CF locus (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: The Φ value data suggest strain in the region of the main CF locus.
source: In this background, Φ value analysis detected a clear temporal gradient in opening-related movements which spreads along the longitudinal, cytoplasmic to extracellular, protein axis from catalytic site 2 towards the pore (Figure 1C): in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized (Φ ~ 1 for position 1246), the NBD-TMD interface is on the move (Φ ~ 0.5 for position 275), whereas the pore is still shut (Φ ~ 0.2 for position 348), suggesting strain in the region of the main CF locus (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the Φ value data supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: Early movement within catalytic site 2 was suggested by the large Φ value for position 1246 in the Walker A motif of NBD2.
source: Early movement within catalytic site 2 was suggested by the large Φ value for position 1246 in the Walker A motif of NBD2 (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: Position 555 is near the NBD1 signature sequence.
source: To test timing of movements at the opposing NBD1 surface of catalytic site 2, we targeted position 555 (Figure 1A,C–D, red) near the NBD1 signature sequence: the R555 and T1246 side chains span the site 2 interface (Figure 1D, lower dotted ellipse) to form a hydrogen bond in open CFTR channels (Vergani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on structural information.

claim: The R555 and T1246 side chains span the site 2 interface to form a hydrogen bond in open CFTR channels.
source: To test timing of movements at the opposing NBD1 surface of catalytic site 2, we targeted position 555 (Figure 1A,C–D, red) near the NBD1 signature sequence: the R555 and T1246 side chains span the site 2 interface (Figure 1D, lower dotted ellipse) to form a hydrogen bond in open CFTR channels (Vergani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: Three tested arbitrary substitutions (glutamine, alanine, cysteine) of the native arginine at position 555 all dramatically lowered channel activity.
source: Three tested arbitrary substitutions (see Materials and methods) of the native arginine at position 555 of our background construct (glutamine, alanine, cysteine) all dramatically lowered channel activity (Figure 2A): open probability (Po) in saturating (10 mM) ATP was reduced by up to 10-fold (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: Open probability (Po) in saturating (10 mM) ATP was reduced by up to 10-fold for position 555 mutants.
source: Three tested arbitrary substitutions (see Materials and methods) of the native arginine at position 555 of our background construct (glutamine, alanine, cysteine) all dramatically lowered channel activity (Figure 2A): open probability (Po) in saturating (10 mM) ATP was reduced by up to 10-fold (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The graded reduction in the closed-open equilibrium constant (Keq) for position 555 mutants was caused predominantly by mutational effects on mean interburst durations (τib) which were prolonged by up to 10-fold.
source: This graded reduction in the closed-open equilibrium constant (Keq) was caused predominantly by mutational effects on mean interburst durations (τib) which were prolonged by up to 10-fold (Figure 2C), reporting large reductions in channel opening rate (kCO = 1/τib).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 10 mM ATP remained saturating for all of the position 555 mutants.
source: Importantly, since 10 mM ATP remained saturating for all of the mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, red bars), this reduced rate kCO indeed reflects slowing of the C1→O1 step (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mean open burst durations (τb) for position 555 mutants were shortened by less than twofold.
source: In contrast, mean open burst durations (τb) were shortened by less than twofold (Figure 2B), reporting only modest effects of the mutations on channel closing rate (kOC = 1/τb).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Position 117 is in the first extracellular loop, where mutations affect gating and are associated with CF.
source: To further expand the longitudinal axial distance spanned by our target positions, we also studied position 117 (Figure 1A,C, blue) in the first extracellular loop, where mutations affect gating and are associated with CF (Sheppard et al., 1993; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sheppard et al., 1993 and Yu et al., 2016.

claim: Substitution of glutamine, alanine, histidine, or cysteine into position 117 all robustly reduced Po by up to ~30 fold.
source: Beside a modest reduction in unitary conductance due to the removal of the positive charge of the native arginine, substitution of glutamine, alanine, histidine, or cysteine into position 117 all robustly reduced Po (Figure 2F), by up to ~30 fold (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2F and 2I.

claim: The reduced Po for position 117 mutants reflected a parallel reduction in mean open burst durations, by >50 fold for the histidine and cysteine substitutions.
source: However, compared to the position 555 mutants, the kinetic pattern of gating of the position 117 mutants was strikingly different (cf., Figure 2F and A): the reduced Po in this case reflected a parallel reduction in mean open burst durations, by >50 fold for the histidine and cysteine substitutions (Figure 2G), whereas mean interburst durations remained largely unaffected (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mean interburst durations for position 117 mutants remained largely unaffected.
source: However, compared to the position 555 mutants, the kinetic pattern of gating of the position 117 mutants was strikingly different (cf., Figure 2F and A): the reduced Po in this case reflected a parallel reduction in mean open burst durations, by >50 fold for the histidine and cysteine substitutions (Figure 2G), whereas mean interburst durations remained largely unaffected (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Perturbations at position 117 selectively affect channel closing, but not opening, rate.
source: Thus, perturbations at position 117 selectively affect channel closing, but not opening, rate, yielding a Brønsted plot with a slope of essentially zero (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The Φ value for position 117 is 0.05 ± 0.02.
source: The extremely low value of Φ = 0.05 ± 0.02 for position 117 implies very late movement of this extracellular position during pore opening, indicating that the conformational wave that begins in catalytic site 2 ends at the extracellular surface.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: The extremely low Φ value for position 117 implies very late movement of this extracellular position during pore opening.
source: The extremely low value of Φ = 0.05 ± 0.02 for position 117 implies very late movement of this extracellular position during pore opening, indicating that the conformational wave that begins in catalytic site 2 ends at the extracellular surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: The conformational wave that begins in catalytic site 2 ends at the extracellular surface.
source: The extremely low value of Φ = 0.05 ± 0.02 for position 117 implies very late movement of this extracellular position during pore opening, indicating that the conformational wave that begins in catalytic site 2 ends at the extracellular surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: For low-Po mutants, channel numbers were estimated at the end of each experiment by exposure to 2'-deoxy-ATP (dATP) or 2'-deoxy-N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-dATP) which markedly stimulated channel open probability.
source: Because accurate estimation of opening rate requires correct estimation of the number of active channels in the patch, which is difficult when the Po is small, even with very long recordings, for low-Po mutants like those in Figure 2A and F channel numbers were estimated at the end of each experiment by exposure to 2'-deoxy-ATP (dATP) or 2'-deoxy-N6-(2-phenylethyl)-ATP (P-dATP) which markedly stimulated channel open probability (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a methodological approach used in the study, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For all mutants studied, the reconstructed interburst ↔ burst sequences obtained in saturating ATP were reasonably described by a two-step process.
source: Of note, for all mutants studied here the reconstructed interburst ↔ burst sequences obtained in saturating ATP (cf., Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were reasonably described by a two-step process, as confirmed by dwell-time analysis (see example histograms for 117 and 555 position mutants in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on dwell-time analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Position 1348 is in the NBD2 signature sequence.
source: To address timing of movements in non-catalytic site 1, we first targeted positon 1348 in the NBD2 signature sequence (Figure 1A,C–D, orange).
evidence: This is based on structural information.

claim: Replacement of the native histidine at position 1348 with an alanine increased Po.
source: Replacement of the native histidine at position 1348 with an alanine increased Po, whereas substitutions by methionine, tyrosine, or glutamate decreased it (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: Substitutions of position 1348 by methionine, tyrosine, or glutamate decreased Po.
source: Replacement of the native histidine at position 1348 with an alanine increased Po, whereas substitutions by methionine, tyrosine, or glutamate decreased it (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: Changes in Po for position 1348 mutants reflected simultaneous changes in both mean burst and interburst durations.
source: In both cases however, changes in Po reflected simultaneous changes in both mean burst and interburst durations (Figure 3B,C; cf., histograms in Figure 3—figure supplement 1): that is, shortened bursts typically coupled with prolonged interbursts (H1348E/Y; Figure 3A–C), or prolonged bursts coupled with shortened interbursts (H1348A; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Perturbations at position 1348 alter both opening and closing rates.
source: Thus, perturbations at position 1348 alter both opening and closing rates, yielding a Brønsted plot with an intermediate slope (Figure 3E): the value of Φ = 0.42 ± 0.04 stands in stark contrast to Φ ~ 1 for catalytic site 2, and indicates delayed motion at position 1348, relative to site 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Φ value for position 1348 is 0.42 ± 0.04.
source: Thus, perturbations at position 1348 alter both opening and closing rates, yielding a Brønsted plot with an intermediate slope (Figure 3E): the value of Φ = 0.42 ± 0.04 stands in stark contrast to Φ ~ 1 for catalytic site 2, and indicates delayed motion at position 1348, relative to site 2.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Φ value of 0.42 ± 0.04 for position 1348 indicates delayed motion at position 1348, relative to site 2.
source: Thus, perturbations at position 1348 alter both opening and closing rates, yielding a Brønsted plot with an intermediate slope (Figure 3E): the value of Φ = 0.42 ± 0.04 stands in stark contrast to Φ ~ 1 for catalytic site 2, and indicates delayed motion at position 1348, relative to site 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: Position 460 is in the NBD1 Walker A motif, corresponding to position 1246 in ATP site 2.
source: To target the opposing, NBD1 surface of non-catalytic site 1, we chose position 460 in the NBD1 Walker A motif, corresponding to position 1246 in ATP site 2 (Figure 1A,C–D, orange).
evidence: This is based on structural information.

claim: Positions 460 and 1348 flank non-catalytic site 1 from two sides.
source: Positions 460 and 1348 flank non-catalytic site 1 (Figure 1D, upper dotted ellipse) from two sides.
evidence: This is based on structural information shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The alanine, serine, and proline substitutions at position 460 markedly reduced Po.
source: Relative to the native threonine at positions 460, the alanine, serine, and proline substitutions markedly reduced Po (Figure 3F,I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3I.

claim: Changes in Po for position 460 mutants reflected coupled opposing changes in mean burst and interburst durations.
source: As with position 1348, these changes in Po again reflected coupled opposing changes in mean burst and interburst durations (Figure 3G,H; cf., histograms in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: The Φ value for position 460 is 0.36 ± 0.07.
source: Correspondingly, the Brønsted plot for position 460 (Figure 3J) revealed a low-intermediate value of Φ = 0.36 ± 0.07, corroborating the conclusion from position 1348 that movement within non-catalytic site 1 during pore opening is markedly delayed compared to that within catalytic site 2.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Movement within non-catalytic site 1 during pore opening is markedly delayed compared to that within catalytic site 2.
source: Correspondingly, the Brønsted plot for position 460 (Figure 3J) revealed a low-intermediate value of Φ = 0.36 ± 0.07, corroborating the conclusion from position 1348 that movement within non-catalytic site 1 during pore opening is markedly delayed compared to that within catalytic site 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data from positions 460 and 1348.

claim: 10 mM ATP remained saturating for all site-1 mutants.
source: Importantly, although perturbations of the NBD1 Walker A motif might impair ATP binding at non-catalytic site 1 (Vergani et al., 2003), 10 mM ATP remained saturating for all of our site-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, orange bars).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The large Φ of positions in catalytic site 2 but low-to-intermediate Φ of positions in non-catalytic site 1 implies that timing of movements in the two ATP sites during pore opening is highly asymmetric.
source: The large Φ of positions in catalytic site 2 but low-to-intermediate Φ of positions in non-catalytic site 1 implies that timing of movements in the two ATP sites during pore opening is highly asymmetric: whereas catalytic site 2 has already adopted its open-like conformation in the T state, non-catalytic site 1 is still on the move.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: Whereas catalytic site 2 has already adopted its open-like conformation in the T state, non-catalytic site 1 is still on the move.
source: The large Φ of positions in catalytic site 2 but low-to-intermediate Φ of positions in non-catalytic site 1 implies that timing of movements in the two ATP sites during pore opening is highly asymmetric: whereas catalytic site 2 has already adopted its open-like conformation in the T state, non-catalytic site 1 is still on the move.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: CH1 and CH2 are located closer to non-catalytic site 1, whereas CH3 and CH4 closer to catalytic site 2.
source: If the movements completed in non-catalytic site 1 between the T state and open state are large-scale rearrangements, then a similarly pronounced temporal asymmetry of motions might be detectable one structural level further along the axis, at the level of the four coupling helices (Figure 1C, violet helices), since CH1 and CH2 are located closer to non-catalytic site 1, whereas CH3 and CH4 closer to catalytic site 2 (Figure 1D, violet helices).
evidence: This is based on structural information shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Substitutions at positions 172, 961, and 1068 caused both increases and decreases in open probability.
source: At positions 172, 961, and 1068 (the native residues are leucine, methionine, and phenylalanine, respectively) substitutions caused both increases and decreases in open probability (Figure 4D,I,N), and the underlying changes in gating pattern were similar (Figure 4A,F,K): a clear trend for an association of lengthened bursts with shortened interbursts and of shortened bursts with lengthened interbursts could be observed (compare Figs. B-C, G-H, L-M; cf., histograms in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Perturbations at positions 172, 961, and 1068 affect opening and closing rates in opposite directions but to comparable extents.
source: Thus, perturbations at positions 172, 961, and 1068 affect opening and closing rates in opposite directions but to comparable extents, yielding Brønsted plots with intermediate slopes in each case (Figure 4E,J,O), indicating that in the T state the coupling helices have already left their closed-like, but have not yet reached their final open-like, positions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 4E, J, and O.

claim: In the T state the coupling helices have already left their closed-like, but have not yet reached their final open-like, positions.
source: Thus, perturbations at positions 172, 961, and 1068 affect opening and closing rates in opposite directions but to comparable extents, yielding Brønsted plots with intermediate slopes in each case (Figure 4E,J,O), indicating that in the T state the coupling helices have already left their closed-like, but have not yet reached their final open-like, positions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: The Φ value for position 172 is 0.51 ± 0.07.
source: On the other hand, the obtained values of Φ = 0.51 ± 0.07 for position 172, Φ = 0.60 ± 0.12 for position 961, and Φ = 0.54 ± 0.07 for position 1068 are quite similar to each other and to Φ = 0.50 ± 0.13 for position 275 (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: The Φ value for position 961 is 0.60 ± 0.12.
source: On the other hand, the obtained values of Φ = 0.51 ± 0.07 for position 172, Φ = 0.60 ± 0.12 for position 961, and Φ = 0.54 ± 0.07 for position 1068 are quite similar to each other and to Φ = 0.50 ± 0.13 for position 275 (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: The Φ value for position 1068 is 0.54 ± 0.07.
source: On the other hand, the obtained values of Φ = 0.51 ± 0.07 for position 172, Φ = 0.60 ± 0.12 for position 961, and Φ = 0.54 ± 0.07 for position 1068 are quite similar to each other and to Φ = 0.50 ± 0.13 for position 275 (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: The Φ value for position 275 is 0.50 ± 0.13.
source: On the other hand, the obtained values of Φ = 0.51 ± 0.07 for position 172, Φ = 0.60 ± 0.12 for position 961, and Φ = 0.54 ± 0.07 for position 1068 are quite similar to each other and to Φ = 0.50 ± 0.13 for position 275 (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: Position 508, the locus of the most common (>70%) CF mutation, is found in a surface cleft of NBD1 which accommodates CH4 to form a joint-like interface in which the F508 side chain interacts with aromatic CH4 residues, including F1068.
source: Position 508 (Figure 1A,C–D, deep purple), the locus of the most common (>70%) CF mutation, is found in a surface cleft of NBD1 which accommodates CH4 to form a joint-like interface in which the F508 side chain interacts with aromatic CH4 residues, including F1068 (Zhang and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang and Chen, 2016.

claim: Deletion of phenylalanine 508 is detrimental for folding and stability of the CFTR protein.
source: Deletion of phenylalanine 508 is detrimental for folding and stability of the CFTR protein (Du et al., 2005; Okiyoneda et al., 2010), but also severely impairs gating (Miki et al., 2010; Kopeikin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Du et al., 2005 and Okiyoneda et al., 2010.

claim: Deletion of phenylalanine 508 severely impairs gating.
source: Deletion of phenylalanine 508 is detrimental for folding and stability of the CFTR protein (Du et al., 2005; Okiyoneda et al., 2010), but also severely impairs gating (Miki et al., 2010; Kopeikin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miki et al., 2010 and Kopeikin et al., 2014.

claim: Replacement of the native phenylalanine at position 508 with cysteine, leucine, and serine all markedly reduced open probability.
source: To address timing of motions in this disease hotspot-position, we replaced the native phenylalanine with cysteine, leucine, and serine. All substitutions markedly reduced open probability (Figure 5A,D), supporting exquisite sensitivity of this region to structural perturbations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5D.

claim: The reduction in the closed-open equilibrium constant for position 508 mutants was caused in each case by a simultaneous shortening of mean burst and lengthening of mean interburst durations, which were comparably affected.
source: The reduction in the closed-open equilibrium constant was caused in each case by a simultaneous shortening of mean burst and lengthening of mean interburst durations, which were comparably affected (Figure 5B–C; cf., histograms in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The Φ value for position 508 is 0.55 ± 0.02.
source: The resulting Φ = 0.55 ± 0.02 (Figure 5E) is indistinguishable from that of position 1068, and indicates that position 508 is also just on the move in the T state for opening.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Position 508 is just on the move in the T state for opening.
source: The resulting Φ = 0.55 ± 0.02 (Figure 5E) is indistinguishable from that of position 1068, and indicates that position 508 is also just on the move in the T state for opening.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: The reduced opening rate of the position 508 mutants was not due to impaired ATP binding, as 10 mM ATP remained saturating.
source: Again, importantly, the reduced opening rate of the position 508 mutants was not due to impaired ATP binding, as 10 mM ATP remained saturating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, deep purple bars).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: X-ray or cryo-EM structures may capture stable closed and open ground states.
source: Whereas X-ray or cryo-EM structures may capture stable closed (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017) and open ground states, the structure of the transition state traversed during opening, and the relative timing of motions in various protein regions may presently be inferred only from Φ value analysis (Auerbach, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017; and Auerbach, 2007.

claim: The structure of the transition state traversed during opening, and the relative timing of motions in various protein regions may presently be inferred only from Φ value analysis.
source: Whereas X-ray or cryo-EM structures may capture stable closed (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017) and open ground states, the structure of the transition state traversed during opening, and the relative timing of motions in various protein regions may presently be inferred only from Φ value analysis (Auerbach, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Auerbach, 2007.

claim: Previous work revealed a Φ value gradient along the longitudinal protein axis, suggesting that the opening conformational change spreads from catalytic site 2 towards the pore.
source: Previous work revealed a Φ value gradient along the longitudinal protein axis, suggesting that the opening conformational change spreads from catalytic site 2 towards the pore (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: By expanding the axial distance spanned by target positions, a gradient of Φ values from ~1 for both sides of catalytic ATP site 2, all the way to ~0 for the extracellular protein surface was shown.
source: By expanding the axial distance spanned by our target positions here we show a gradient of Φ values from ~1 for both sides of catalytic ATP site 2, all the way to ~0 for the extracellular protein surface (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: These findings corroborate the earlier proposal that in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized but the pore is still in its closed-like (inward-facing) conformation.
source: These findings corroborate the earlier proposal that in the T state catalytic site 2 is already dimerized but the pore is still in its closed-like (inward-facing) conformation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: Phenylalanine 508, the locus of the most common CF mutation, is located at the NBD-TMD interface.
source: Phenylalanine 508, the locus of the most common CF mutation, is located at the NBD-TMD interface, that is, in a region expected to experience strain in the T state.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge.

claim: Position 508 is in a region expected to experience strain in the T state.
source: Phenylalanine 508, the locus of the most common CF mutation, is located at the NBD-TMD interface, that is, in a region expected to experience strain in the T state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Φ value gradient.

claim: Position 508 is just on the move in the T state, together with spatially adjacent CH4, as reported by their intermediate, essentially indistinguishable Φ values of ~0.5.
source: Here we show that position 508 is indeed just on the move in the T state, together with spatially adjacent CH4 (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017), as reported by their intermediate, essentially indistinguishable Φ values of ~0.5 (Figures 4O and 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figures 4O and 5E.

claim: All tested perturbations of the F508 side chain reduce opening and accelerate non-hydrolytic closing rate.
source: Because all tested perturbations of the F508 side chain reduce opening and accelerate non-hydrolytic closing rate (Figure 5B–C), the simplest interpretation is that the native phenylalanine side chain is involved in stabilizing interactions that become stronger as the closed channel reaches the T state, and even stronger when it relaxes to the open state.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The native phenylalanine side chain at position 508 is involved in stabilizing interactions that become stronger as the closed channel reaches the T state, and even stronger when it relaxes to the open state.
source: Because all tested perturbations of the F508 side chain reduce opening and accelerate non-hydrolytic closing rate (Figure 5B–C), the simplest interpretation is that the native phenylalanine side chain is involved in stabilizing interactions that become stronger as the closed channel reaches the T state, and even stronger when it relaxes to the open state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Mutations at position 508 dramatically reduce protein stability.
source: The alternative explanation that the native phenylalanine side chain forms destabilizing interaction(s) in the closed state seems unlikely, as mutations here dramatically reduce protein stability, suggesting an overall stabilizing role for residue F508 in its native environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about F508 mutations.

claim: In wild-type (WT) CFTR the hydrolytic pathway for channel closure is much faster than the non-hydrolytic pathway.
source: Of note, because in wild-type (WT) CFTR the hydrolytic pathway for channel closure is much faster than the non-hydrolytic pathway, the strong acceleration of non-hydrolytic closing rate by deletion or substitutions of residue F508 is not apparent when studied in a WT (hydrolytic) background (Miki et al., 2010; Kopeikin et al., 2014), a fact that has led to previous misassignment of a Φ value close to 1 for position 508 (Aleksandrov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miki et al., 2010; Kopeikin et al., 2014; and Aleksandrov et al., 2009.

claim: Mutation R117H is associated with a mild form of CF and causes, beside a moderate reduction in single channel chloride conductance, a strong channel gating defect.
source: Mutation R117H is associated with a mild form of CF and causes, beside a moderate reduction in single channel chloride conductance, a strong channel gating defect (Sheppard et al., 1993; Yu et al., 2016), suggesting that this position is involved in interactions that change in a gating-state dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sheppard et al., 1993 and Yu et al., 2016.

claim: All substitutions at position 117 dramatically reduced open probability by accelerating closure while leaving opening unaffected.
source: Indeed, all substitutions at position 117 dramatically reduced open probability (Figure 2I) by accelerating closure (Figure 2G) while leaving opening unaffected (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 2G, H, and I.

claim: In closed-state structures of CFTR the native R117 side chain is not seen to form strong interactions with other residues.
source: Because in closed-state structures of CFTR the native R117 side chain is not seen to form strong interactions with other residues (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017), the implication is that it forms a stabilizing interaction (or interactions) in the open state, that is (are) lost when the arginine at position 117 is replaced.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang and Chen, 2016 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The native R117 side chain forms a stabilizing interaction (or interactions) in the open state, that is (are) lost when the arginine at position 117 is replaced.
source: Because in closed-state structures of CFTR the native R117 side chain is not seen to form strong interactions with other residues (Zhang and Chen, 2016; Liu et al., 2017), the implication is that it forms a stabilizing interaction (or interactions) in the open state, that is (are) lost when the arginine at position 117 is replaced.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural information and experimental data.

claim: The stabilizing interaction of R117 is not yet formed in the T state: its appearance is among the last movements associated with pore opening (Φ ~ 0).
source: Furthermore, the stabilizing interaction is not yet formed in the T state: its appearance is among the last movements associated with pore opening (Φ ~ 0).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: R117 substitutions selectively destabilize the open state, but not the transition state, relative to the closed state, as indicated by the unaltered opening rate.
source: Thus, R117 substitutions selectively destabilize the open state, but not the transition state, relative to the closed state, as indicated by the unaltered opening rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Unlike catalytic site 2 which has already adopted its open-like conformation in the T state, non-catalytic site 1 is still on the move between its closed- and open-like conformations.
source: In striking contrast to the large Φ values of positions on both sides of the dimer interface in catalytic site 2, positions flanking non-catalytic site 1 display low-to-intermediate Φ values (Figure 6A, orange vs. red residues (left) and numbers (right)). Thus, unlike catalytic site 2 which has already adopted its open-like conformation (Figure 6A, right, red residues) in the T state, non-catalytic site 1 is still on the move between its closed- and open-like conformations (Figure 6A, left and right, orange residues).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pronounced asymmetry in the timing of motions at one end of the dimer interface compared to the other cannot be detected at the level of the four coupling helices, which are all characterized by Φ values of 0.5–0.6.
source: Interestingly, such pronounced asymmetry in the timing of motions at one end of the dimer interface compared to the other cannot be detected at the level of the four coupling helices, which are all characterized by Φ values of 0.5–0.6 (Figure 6A, violet residues (left) and numbers (right)).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The movements that take place in non-catalytic site 1 between the T state and the open state likely remain confined to the site-1 interface.
source: Thus, the movements that take place in non-catalytic site 1 between the T state and the open state likely remain confined to the site-1 interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Φ value data.

claim: ATP bound at the two composite sites acts as molecular glue that stabilizes the open-pore conformation by bonding the NBD interfaces together.
source: ATP bound at the two composite sites acts as molecular glue that stabilizes the open-pore conformation by bonding the NBD interfaces together (Moody et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moody et al., 2002 and Smith et al., 2002.

claim: The data suggest a division of labor in the bonding activities of the two ATP sites.
source: Our data suggest a division of labor in the bonding activities of the two sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Phosphorylated WT CFTR channels open infrequently even in the absence of ATP.
source: Phosphorylated WT CFTR channels open infrequently even in the absence of ATP (Figure 6B, top current trace), and such 'spontaneous' openings reflect occasional dimerization of empty, unliganded NBDs (Mihályi et al., 2016) (Figure 6B, top cartoon).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mihályi et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Spontaneous openings of WT CFTR reflect occasional dimerization of empty, unliganded NBDs.
source: Phosphorylated WT CFTR channels open infrequently even in the absence of ATP (Figure 6B, top current trace), and such 'spontaneous' openings reflect occasional dimerization of empty, unliganded NBDs (Mihályi et al., 2016) (Figure 6B, top cartoon).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mihályi et al., 2016.

claim: Comparison of spontaneous gating of WT channels with the equilibrium gating of a hydrolysis-deficient mutant (K1250R) in saturating ATP reveals two robust effects of bound ATP: a shortening of closed interburst durations and a lengthening of open burst durations, both by >100 fold.
source: Comparison of such spontaneous gating of WT channels with the equilibrium gating of a hydrolysis-deficient mutant, such as the NBD2 Walker A lysine mutant K1250R, in saturating ATP (Figure 6B, bottom current trace) reveals two robust effects of bound ATP: a shortening of closed interburst durations (Figure 6B, compare green bars above current traces) and a lengthening of open burst durations (Figure 6B, compare red bars below current traces), both by >100 fold (Mihályi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mihályi et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Bound ATP reduces the energetic barrier for opening, but increases the barrier for non-hydrolytic closure.
source: Thus, bound ATP reduces the energetic barrier for opening, but increases the barrier for non-hydrolytic closure (Figure 6C, black vs. orange standard Gibbs energy profiles).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: In the T state catalytic site 2 has already finished moving, that is, the site-2 glue is already bonded.
source: Which of the two bound ATP molecules affects opening rate? Our Φ value analysis indicates that in the T state catalytic site 2 has already finished moving, that is, the site-2 glue is already bonded (Figure 6B, bottom cartoon, lower site; red semi-circles in states T and O1): that bonding readily explains the reduction in the energetic barrier for opening, that is, stimulation of opening rate, by ATP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Bonding of the site-2 glue readily explains the reduction in the energetic barrier for opening, that is, stimulation of opening rate, by ATP.
source: Which of the two bound ATP molecules affects opening rate? Our Φ value analysis indicates that in the T state catalytic site 2 has already finished moving, that is, the site-2 glue is already bonded (Figure 6B, bottom cartoon, lower site; red semi-circles in states T and O1): that bonding readily explains the reduction in the energetic barrier for opening, that is, stimulation of opening rate, by ATP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data.

claim: Because the site-2 glue is bonded both in the T and O1 states, it cannot affect the height of the barrier for non-hydrolytic closure.
source: Which of the two bound ATP molecules affects non-hydrolytic closing rate? Because it is bonded both in the T and O1 states, the site-2 glue cannot affect the height of the barrier for non-hydrolytic closure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Φ value data.

claim: The low Φ value of non-catalytic site 1 indicates localized movements between the T state and the open state, which reflects tight bonding of the site-1 glue (i.e., tightening of the site-1 interface).
source: On the other hand, the low Φ value of non-catalytic site 1 indicates localized movements between the T state and the open state, which we propose reflects tight bonding of the site-1 glue (i.e., tightening of the site-1 interface; Figure 6B, bottom cartoon, upper site; red semi-circle only in state O1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Φ value data illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: By selectively stabilizing the open state relative to the T state, the site-1 glue increases the height of the barrier for non-hydrolytic closure, explaining the observed prolongation of non-hydrolytic bursts by ATP.
source: By selectively stabilizing the open state relative to the T state, the site-1 glue increases the height of the barrier for non-hydrolytic closure, explaining the observed prolongation of non-hydrolytic bursts by ATP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In the context of the functional cycle of WT CFTR, ATP bound at catalytic site 2 promotes efficient opening (speeds step C1→O1).
source: In the context of the functional cycle of WT CFTR (Figure 1B) ATP bound at catalytic site 2 promotes efficient opening (speeds step C1→O1) whereas ATP bound at non-catalytic site 1, by slowing rate O1→C1, ensures progress through ATP hydrolysis: such unidirectional cycling is essential for ABC proteins to mediate uphill transport.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in the context of the functional cycle.

claim: ATP bound at non-catalytic site 1, by slowing rate O1→C1, ensures progress through ATP hydrolysis.
source: In the context of the functional cycle of WT CFTR (Figure 1B) ATP bound at catalytic site 2 promotes efficient opening (speeds step C1→O1) whereas ATP bound at non-catalytic site 1, by slowing rate O1→C1, ensures progress through ATP hydrolysis: such unidirectional cycling is essential for ABC proteins to mediate uphill transport.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in the context of the functional cycle.

claim: Unidirectional cycling is essential for ABC proteins to mediate uphill transport.
source: In the context of the functional cycle of WT CFTR (Figure 1B) ATP bound at catalytic site 2 promotes efficient opening (speeds step C1→O1) whereas ATP bound at non-catalytic site 1, by slowing rate O1→C1, ensures progress through ATP hydrolysis: such unidirectional cycling is essential for ABC proteins to mediate uphill transport.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC protein function.

claim: In asymmetric ABC proteins flipping to the outward-facing, NBD-dimerized conformation is followed by a step in which the consensus site becomes committed to ATP hydrolysis.
source: In asymmetric ABC proteins flipping to the outward-facing, NBD-dimerized conformation is followed by a step in which the consensus site becomes committed to ATP hydrolysis (Timachi et al., 2017): that step might involve bonding of the glue in the non-catalytic site.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Timachi et al., 2017.

claim: The step in which the consensus site becomes committed to ATP hydrolysis might involve bonding of the glue in the non-catalytic site.
source: In asymmetric ABC proteins flipping to the outward-facing, NBD-dimerized conformation is followed by a step in which the consensus site becomes committed to ATP hydrolysis (Timachi et al., 2017): that step might involve bonding of the glue in the non-catalytic site.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with the functional cross-talk between the two sites observed in CFTR or related MRP1.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the functional cross-talk between the two sites observed in CFTR or related MRP1 (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999; Gao et al., 2000; Hou et al., 2002): perturbations in the non-catalytic site of CFTR reduce the ATPase turnover rate of the catalytic site (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999) by lowering the fraction of open bursts that are terminated by ATP hydrolysis as opposed to non-hydrolytic dissociation of the NBD dimer (Csanády et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramjeesingh et al., 1999; Gao et al., 2000; Hou et al., 2002; and Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: Perturbations in the non-catalytic site of CFTR reduce the ATPase turnover rate of the catalytic site by lowering the fraction of open bursts that are terminated by ATP hydrolysis as opposed to non-hydrolytic dissociation of the NBD dimer.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the functional cross-talk between the two sites observed in CFTR or related MRP1 (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999; Gao et al., 2000; Hou et al., 2002): perturbations in the non-catalytic site of CFTR reduce the ATPase turnover rate of the catalytic site (Ramjeesingh et al., 1999) by lowering the fraction of open bursts that are terminated by ATP hydrolysis as opposed to non-hydrolytic dissociation of the NBD dimer (Csanády et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramjeesingh et al., 1999 and Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: The hydrolysis-disrupting D1370N mutation precludes targeting position 1370 for Φ value analysis.
source: The hydrolysis-disrupting D1370N mutation, an essential component of our background construct, precludes targeting position 1370 for Φ value analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation of the study.

claim: The non-hydrolytic closing rate of D1370N CFTR channels is substantially faster than that of other non-hydrolytic catalytic site-2 mutants, suggesting that this mutation affects not only opening, but also non-hydrolytic closing rate.
source: However, the non-hydrolytic closing rate of D1370N CFTR channels is substantially faster than that of other non-hydrolytic catalytic site-2 mutants, suggesting that this mutation affects not only opening, but also non-hydrolytic closing rate (Gunderson and Kopito, 1995; Vergani et al., 2003): the implication is that the Φ value of position 1370 might be lower than those of the catalytic site-2 positions studied here.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gunderson and Kopito, 1995 and Vergani et al., 2003.

claim: The Φ value of position 1370 might be lower than those of the catalytic site-2 positions studied here.
source: However, the non-hydrolytic closing rate of D1370N CFTR channels is substantially faster than that of other non-hydrolytic catalytic site-2 mutants, suggesting that this mutation affects not only opening, but also non-hydrolytic closing rate (Gunderson and Kopito, 1995; Vergani et al., 2003): the implication is that the Φ value of position 1370 might be lower than those of the catalytic site-2 positions studied here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic properties of the D1370N mutant.

claim: Aspartate 1370 is physically located in between the two ATP sites, in the center of the NBD interface, at the boundary between core and α-helical subdomains of NBD2.
source: Although functionally involved in Mg2+ coordination in catalytic site 2 (cf., Zaitseva et al., 2005), aspartate 1370 is physically located in between the two ATP sites, in the center of the NBD interface, at the boundary between core and α-helical subdomains of NBD2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, salmon).
evidence: This is based on structural information shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aspartate 1370 is in contact with the conserved Q-loop glutamine Q1291.
source: Moreover, it is in contact with the conserved Q-loop glutamine Q1291 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, yellow) (Liu et al., 2017) which acts as a γ-phosphate sensor to induce an ~15o rotation of the α-helical subdomain towards the core subdomain upon ATP binding (Karpowich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017 and Karpowich et al., 2001, and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Q1291 acts as a γ-phosphate sensor to induce an ~15° rotation of the α-helical subdomain towards the core subdomain upon ATP binding.

claim: Residue D1370 might be involved in subdomain closure, essential for stable NBD dimerization.
source: Thus, residue D1370 might also be involved in subdomain closure, essential for stable NBD dimerization (Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Smith et al., 2002.

claim: The Φ value map obtained supports distinct roles for the two composite ATP sites in CFTR channel gating and reveal the molecular mechanism of the gating defects caused by two common CF mutations.
source: In conclusion, the Φ value map obtained here supports distinct roles for the two composite ATP sites in CFTR channel gating and reveal the molecular mechanism of the gating defects caused by two common CF mutations.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: Clarifying the extent of movements in the two ATP sites during each step in the channel opening/closing cycle will require comparisons among high-resolution structures of CFTR trapped in phosphorylated closed- and open-channel states.
source: Whereas this work reports relative timing of movements in the two ATP sites during pore opening, clarifying the extent of these movements during each step in the channel opening/closing cycle will require comparisons among high-resolution structures of CFTR trapped in phosphorylated closed- and open-channel states.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The recent structures of unphosphorylated closed and phosphorylated occluded CFTR have just started to set the stage for such comparisons.
source: The recent structures of unphosphorylated closed (Liu et al., 2017) and phosphorylated occluded (Zhang et al., 2017) CFTR have just started to set the stage for such comparisons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2017.
